en: *The Ten Precepts for Śrāmaṇeras and Their Ritual Deportment*, one fascicle;
translator lost, appended to the Eastern Jin Record.
The Buddha said to Śāriputra: "Go and ordain Rāhula to leave the household life. Śāriputra replied:
"How shall I be delivered?
The Buddha taught him, saying:
"I, Rāhula, take refuge in the Buddha, take refuge in the Dharma, and take refuge in the Saṃgha."

Thus it is said three times: "I, [Name], have completed my taking refuge in the Buddha; I have completed my taking refuge in the Dharma; I have completed my taking refuge in the Saṃgha. Thus it is said three times: "For as long as life lasts, I shall not kill;

for as long as life lasts, I shall not steal; for as long as life lasts, I shall not engage in sexual misconduct; for as long as life lasts, I shall not speak falsely; for as long as life lasts, I shall not drink intoxicants. The Blessed One, the Buddha, has gone forth from the household life; I, [Name], following the preceptor [Name], go forth following the Buddha."

Thus it is said three times: "The Buddha, the Blessed One, has gone forth from home, discarded worldly garments, and donned the saffron robe; I, [Name], following the Preceptor [Name], go forth from home in accordance with the Buddha, discarding worldly garments and donning the saffron robe."
"For as long as life lasts, do not kill; observe the śrāmaṇera precepts.
For as long as life lasts, do not steal; observe the śrāmaṇera precepts.
For as long as life lasts, do not engage in sexual misconduct; observe the śrāmaṇera precepts."
"For as long as life lasts, one shall not speak falsely; this is the observance of a śrāmaṇera precept.
For as long as life lasts, one shall not drink intoxicants; this is the observance of a śrāmaṇera precept.
For as long as life lasts, one shall not wear perfumes, garlands, or ornaments, nor anoint the body with scents; this is the observance of a śrāmaṇera precept."
"For as long as life lasts, do not sing, dance, perform, or act as a courtesan, nor go to witness such performances; this is the śrāmaṇera precept.
For as long as life lasts, do not sit on high, wide, or large beds; this is the śrāmaṇera precept."
"For as long as life lasts, do not eat at improper times; this is the śrāmaṇera precept.
For as long as life lasts, do not handle raw gold, silver, or precious objects; this is the śrāmaṇera precept."

"Now that you have completed receiving the ten precepts of a śrāmaṇera, you must wear them upon the crown of your head and uphold them for as long as you live; you must never violate them throughout your life.
You should make offerings to the Triple Gem, and you must not disobey any instruction given by your upādhyāya, ācārya, or anyone else in accordance with the Dharma."
Toward those of superior, middling, and inferior rank, one should always maintain a mind of reverence.

Diligently seek skillful means to practice seated meditation, recite the sutras, and engage in study; encourage others to cultivate merit, thereby closing the gates to the three evil realms and opening the door to Nirvana.
Within the dharma of a bhikṣu, one increases right action and attains the fruits of the four paths.
"The precepts of a śrāmaṇera are: for as long as life lasts, one must not kill or harm any person or creature."

One should mindfully reflect upon the kindness of those from whom one is born, as well as that of teachers and friends; with diligent application, one should practice the Path, desiring to deliver one’s parents.
Be careful never to harbor resentment or engage in litigation; attribute rectitude to others and draw the blame toward yourself.
Regarding the classes of creatures that flutter, wriggle, and crawl, one must not harm or injure them; instead, bestow kindness and relieve their want so that they may find peace.

One should intend to benefit others, never speak of killing, refrain from eating what has been seen to be killed, refrain from eating what has been heard to have been killed, and refrain from eating what is suspected to have been killed.
When you see someone being killed, you should give rise to a mind of compassion and vow: "May I attain the Way so that there shall be no killing in my land.
Do not use plants or trees; be careful not to damage them.
Should one violate this precept, they are no longer a śrāmaṇera.
“The precepts for a śrāmaṇera are: for as long as one lives, one must not steal.

One must not deceive others regarding even a single measure of a *gui*, a *he*, a *zhu*, or a *liang*; one must keep the mind fixed on righteousness and never instruct others to take what is not given.”
One must not, under any circumstances, engage in the buying or selling of servants or slaves, the hiring out of laborers or guests, or the giving away of such persons as gifts.
One must possess no finery, precious playthings, high beds, curtains, or canopies; clothing should merely serve to cover the body and must be devoid of ornamental colors or patterns.
One should take food merely to sustain life and must not indulge in its flavors.

One must not store up grain or hoard impure treasures; if others offer them, one should not accept them, and if they are accepted, they must not be kept but should be distributed to relieve the poor and destitute.
He constantly preached to others the virtue of non-greed, preferring even to have his hand cut off than to take what was not rightfully his.
One who violates this precept is no longer a śrāmaṇera.
"The precepts of a śrāmaṇera require that for as long as life lasts, one must not take a wife or raise offspring."
Guard against distant female beauty and restrain the six sense-faculties; do not look upon beautiful forms.
Let the eyes not gaze about, the mind harbor no thoughts of lust, and the mouth utter no words of flirtation.
Let flowers, perfumes, and cosmetics not come near the body; let pleasant sounds and seductive sights be neither seen nor heard.
It would be better to break one's bones, shatter one's heart, and burn one's body than to commit sexual misconduct;
for though lust gives rise to defilement, it is better to die in chastity than to live in impurity.
If one violates this precept, they are no longer a śrāmaṇera.
"The precepts of a śrāmaṇera take lifelong sincerity and faith as their foundation; one must not engage in double-tongued speech, harsh abuse, lying, or frivolous talk."

Do not praise others in one's presence and disparage them behind their back; when testifying, do not lead others into guilt. Speak slowly and maintain integrity, refraining from proclaiming the faults of others. When preaching the Dharma to others, ensure your thoughts accord with reason and principle; when seeing those who are disputing, reconcile both sides with kindness.
When a person lives in this world, an axe is held within their mouth; it is by means of their evil speech that they cut themselves.
One who is not careful with their words is no śrāmaṇera.
"The precepts of a śrāmaṇera are: for as long as life lasts, one must not drink alcohol."
One must not taste wine, nor smell it; one must not consume it as gruel, nor give it to others to drink, nor drink medicinal wine, nor stay at an inn where wine is served.
Alcohol is a poisonous water, the primary source of manifold losses; it harms the worthy, destroys the sages, and invites calamity.
That the four immeasurables wither and decay, and that one abandons merit to pursue transgression—all of this does not arise except through it.
"It would be better to drink molten copper than to heedlessly violate the prohibition against alcohol.
Whoever violates this precept is no longer a śrāmaṇera. "The precepts of a śrāmaṇera are:

for as long as life lasts, one must not practice with weapons or handle sharp tools; one must not keep domestic animals or confine birds in cages; one must not drive carriages, ride horses, or indulge in pleasures according to one's whims; and one must not gallop about, go hunting, or shoot at birds and beasts."

Do not set fires to burn mountains and forests, thereby harming living beings; do not breach lakes and ponds or dam up streams and channels; and do not use hooks, fishing lines, or nets to injure aquatic creatures.
One who violates this precept is no longer a śrāmaṇera. Regarding the precepts of a śrāmaṇera:

for as long as life lasts, one must not practice or dabble in board games, *chūpú*, gambling, or betting; nor engage in disputes over winning and losing, dancing, or frivolous jesting; nor chant, sing, or hold musical instruments—such as the *qín*, *sè*, *kōnglóu*, *zhēng*, *dí*, *yú*, or *shēng—to disturb the mind set on the Way.

Do not dig up mountains or marshes, plow fields, cultivate gardens or orchards, plant the five grains, engage in maritime or chariot trade, conduct business in the marketplace, or compete with the common people for profit.

"To violate this precept is to no longer be a śrāmaṇera. Regarding the precepts of a śrāmaṇera: for as long as life lasts, one must not study or practice extraordinary arts, sorcery, medicine, or the way of poisons; nor may one engage in calculating auspicious times, divination, or interpreting signs of good and bad fortune; nor may one look up at the calendar and numbers to calculate the waxing and waning of the moon, lunar and solar eclipses, or the anomalies of the constellations; nor may one concern oneself with mountain collapses, earthquakes, wind, rain, drought, or floods; nor with whether the harvests will be bountiful or poor, or whether there will be pestilence or not—one must not know any of these."
One must not discuss state affairs, weighing their merits and demerits, nor speak of military expeditions, the dispatching of armies, or victory and defeat in offensive warfare.
To violate this precept is to cease being a śrāmaṇera.
"Regarding the precepts for śrāmaṇeras, throughout one's entire life, there must be a distinction between men and women: they shall not reside in the same monastery, nor shall their paths cross.

They shall not travel together in the same boat or carriage, nor engage in conversation when encountered. If they carry different items, they must not examine them; they should distance themselves from suspicion and avoid all doubt."
One should not engage in the exchange of letters, nor borrow, cut, or wash clothing, nor beg for anything.
Even if another offers such things to oneself, one should not accept them.
When intending to travel, one must be accompanied by an elder; one must take care never to travel alone, nor stay, sit, or sleep overnight by oneself.
"To violate this precept is to no longer be a śrāmaṇera.
Regarding the precepts of a śrāmaṇera, for as long as one lives, one shall not befriend those who are not virtuous nor revere those who are not sages.

Sons who are unfilial, butchers, hunters, and those who are thieves or addicted to wine—whose inclinations are perverse and whose conduct is wicked and dangerous—must not be associated with; to engage in such interactions will defile and impair one's progress on the Path."
Dharma robes and alms bowls are always kept close to the body; one does not eat at improper times nor speak what is contrary to the Dharma.
When eating, there is no talking; when lying down, there is no chatter.
One should diligently contemplate the meaning of the teachings, reviewing the old to gain knowledge of the new.
When seated, one should practice meditative contemplation; when rising, one should engage in recitation.
With such observance of the precepts, one is a true disciple of the Buddha.
Having completed the recitation of the precepts, the rules of decorum are next explained: "Having received the ten precepts of a śrāmaṇera, you are a worthy practitioner of the Way."

Next, instruct him as follows: one should proceed gradually, beginning with small matters. He should know the proper deportment and the duties to be performed; he should know the age of his *upādhyāya* and the names of the three teachers. He should be taught to recognize the year, month, and day of his initial reception of the precepts. He should know how many services there are for attending upon the *upādhyāya*, as well as how many services there are for attending upon the *ācārya* according to their respective roles. He should also know how many services there are for providing tooth-sticks and water for washing; he should know how many services there are for handing over the *kāṣāya*, adjusting the *kāṣāya*, and holding the alms bowl; and he should also know how many services there are for holding the *khakkhara* staff and carrying the sandals.

When one is together with an *upādhyāya* or an *ācārya* during a formal invitation, whether arriving at the house of a king, the house of a *gṛhapati*, or the house of a *brāhmaṇa*; whether sitting together for a meal or sitting separately for a meal; whether entering the city together to beg for alms or returning together; when reaching the original location; when it is evening; when eating by the water’s edge, on the roadside, or under a tree; when one goes ahead first while the other waits; when eating from a shared bowl; when exchanging bowls; when eating face-to-face together; when eating one after another; when finished eating and rinsing the mouth; or when departing with the bowl washed—one should fully understand how many matters apply in each case.
It should be known that when serving as a *karmadāna* for the Saṃgha, one must be aware of several matters;
likewise, when one has reached twenty years of age and intends to receive full ordination (*upasampadā*), all such matters must be fully understood.
If, when questioned by a wise bhikṣu, one cannot provide complete answers, one should not be granted full ordination.

Why is this? One who acts as a śrāmaṇera yet does not know the duties and practices appropriate for a śrāmaṇera—such being the case—the affairs of a śramaṇa are difficult to perform and exceedingly subtle.
"Wise śrāmaṇera, you should depart for now and study thoroughly.
You must hear and know everything completely before the full ordination (upasampadā) may be conferred upon you.

As for why you do not understand the dharma of a śrāmaṇera, it is simply because you have not yet realized the suffering of the body and have not subdued your mind, yet you instead wish to receive the full ordination."

Now, as I confer the full precepts upon you, people might say that the Buddha-dharma is easy to practice and that one can easily be a śramaṇa; yet they do not realize that the Way of the Buddha is supremely subtle, and that the operations of demerit and merit, as well as the laws and regulations, are interwoven. To examine you over these several days, it is therefore necessary to first ask these questions.
"If one can fully provide those who are capable and act in accordance with the Dharma, the three masters will be easy to find.
There are five matters for which a master instructs a śrāmaṇera:
first, he should respect the Great Śramaṇa;"
Second, one must not call the Great Śramaṇa by his personal name;
third, when the Great Śramaṇa recites the Prātimokṣa Sūtra, one must not eavesdrop;
fourth, one must not seek out the faults or shortcomings of the Great Śramaṇa.
Fifth, the great śramaṇa must not speak erroneously or fail to act at the proper time;
this constitutes the deportment of a śrāmaṇera.
Furthermore, there are five matters for instructing a śrāmaṇera:
First, one must not revile the Great Śramaṇa in private.
Second, one must not treat the Great Śramaṇa with levity, nor mock him by imitating his speech, gestures, or gait in his presence.
Third, if one sees the Great Śramaṇa passing by, one should immediately rise and stand, or engage in reciting the sūtras;
however, during mealtime or while performing communal tasks, one should not rise.
Fourth, if one encounters a great śramaṇa while walking, one should immediately stop on the path and stand aside to avoid him.
Fifth, if one is engaged in playful jesting, upon seeing a great śramaṇa, one should immediately cease and apologize, saying that one was not aware of his presence.
This is what should be practiced accordingly.
"There are ten matters regarding a śrāmaṇera’s service to his preceptor:
first, he should rise early;..."
Second, when wishing to enter a room, one should first snap the fingers three times;
third, one should provide toothwood and water for rinsing;
fourth, one should offer the *kāṣāya* robe and then offer the sandals.
Fifth, one should sweep the floor and replenish the washing water;
sixth, one should fold the bedding and pillows and wipe down the beds and mats;
seventh, one must not leave the room while the teacher is away and has not yet returned; when the teacher returns, one should go forward to receive his *kāṣāya* and fold it inwardly.
Eighth, if one has committed a transgression, when the preceptor or ācārya instructs and admonishes them, they must not respond with contrary words;
ninth, they should depart while keeping their head bowed to receive the teacher’s words, and should reflect upon them and put them into practice;
tenth, upon leaving the door, they should reach back to pull it closed behind them.
This is the method for serving one's upādhyāya.
"There are five matters for instructing a śrāmaṇera on how to serve an ācārya:
first, one should regard the ācārya in all respects as one regards me;..."
Second, you must not engage in frivolous play;
third, even if they should scold or revile you, you must not retort;
fourth, if they should have you remove a vessel of impurities, you must not spit out in anger.
Fifth, one should perform massage at dusk.
These are the rules for serving an ācārya. Regarding the rules for serving an ācārya:
when a śrāmaṇera serves his teacher, he should rise early and prepare tooth-sticks and water for rinsing.
There are six matters:
first, when cutting the tooth-stick, one should follow the prescribed measurement;
second, one should break off the tip.
Third, one should wash them until they are clean;
fourth, one should discard old, overnight water;
fifth, one should purify the *kamaṇḍalu*.
Sixth, one should enter [the dwelling] carrying a vessel filled with water, ensuring there is no splashing or noise.
This constitutes the complete method for the *yankchi* (tooth-stick) and bathing water.
"There are four matters regarding the bestowing of the *kāṣāya*:
First, one should slowly push it down with one hand while holding it with the other to hand it over;
second, one should next look at both the upper and lower parts;
third, one should remain stationary after having held the teacher’s robe.
"Fourth, one should place it upon the shoulders of the teacher.
This is the method for bestowing the kāṣāya.
There are four matters regarding the gathering of the kāṣāya:"
First, one should inspect the area above and below;
second, one must not allow it to touch the ground;
third, one should place it in its proper, stable location.
Fourth, covering the top.
These are the rules for wearing the *kāṣāya*.
"There are four matters regarding the carrying of the alms bowl:
First, one should wash it until it is clean;
second, wipe it until it is dry;
third, fasten it so that it is secure.
Fourth, one must not allow any sound to be made.
This is the method for carrying the alms bowl.
There are four matters regarding the carrying of the mendicant’s staff (khakkhara):
First, wipe it to remove any impurities;
second, do not place it on the ground so that it makes a sound;
third, you should hand it to the teacher only after he has stepped out of the door.
Fourth, when the teacher returns from outside, one should receive and take it;
whether traveling together, entering the assembly, or prostrating before the Buddha, one should likewise carry and hold it.
This is the method for holding the mendicant’s staff.
"There are four matters regarding the wearing of sandals:
first, one should first shake them out;
second, one should inspect them and then arrange them properly."
Third, one must wash one's hands before handling the *kāṣāya*;
fourth, when the teacher is seated, one should take up the sandals and place them beside him.
These are the rules for handling sandals.
"If one is invited to sit together with the teacher, there are four matters regarding the time of eating while seated in a row:
first, one's seat should be six feet away from the teacher;
second, one should wait until the teacher has finished giving his *dakṣiṇā* (blessing) before presenting one's bowl."
Third, one must not eat rice before the teacher;
fourth, once the teacher has finished eating, one should rise, take the bowl, and place it near oneself.
These are the rules for the mealtime procedure regarding sitting in succession.
"When taking a separate seat for a meal, there are four matters to attend to:
first, one should stand beside the teacher;
second, one should only sit down to eat after the teacher has instructed one to do so."
Third, one should prostrate with the head touching the ground;
fourth, when eating rice, one must not sit haughtily or play about.
Having finished the meal, one should go and stand beside the teacher; only when the teacher instructs one to return to one's seat should one sit.
This is the rule for when sitting separately during a meal.
"When entering a city to beg for alms, there are four matters:
first, one should carry the teacher’s bowl;..."
Second, one should follow behind the teacher and must not step on the teacher’s shadow with one's feet;
third, outside the city, one should take up the bowl and present it to the teacher;
fourth, when entering the city and intending to go elsewhere, one should inform the teacher.
These are the rules for when one goes out to beg for food.
"When returning together to the original place, there are four matters to attend to:
first, one should first slowly open the door and go out to spread out the sitting mat."
Second, having washed the teacher’s hands, one should then withdraw and wash one's own;
third, one should present the bowl to the teacher and then withdraw to stand with palms joined;
fourth, one should prepare in advance the soap powder, hand towel, and other necessary items.
This is the rule for returning to eat at the time of the meal.
When eating by the water's edge, there are four matters:
first, one should seek out a clean spot of ground;
Second, one should seek out grass to make a seat;
third, having taken water to wash the teacher’s hands and then having washed one's own hands, one should then return the bowl to the teacher;
fourth, when the teacher instructs one to eat, one should perform a prostration and then sit back down.
This is the rule for eating by the water's edge.
Regarding the rule for eating under the shade of a tree, there are four matters:
first, one should take the bowl and hang it upon a tree, then gather leaves to make a seat.
Second, he should take water to wash the teacher’s hands; if no water is available, he should take clean grass and offer it to the teacher.
Third, he should return and offer his alms bowl to the teacher.
Fourth, having prepared clean grass in advance to wash the teacher’s bowl, he should then wipe the bowl thoroughly with the grass before departing.
This is the rule for the meal under a tree.
Regarding waiting for one another on the road, there are three matters:
first, place the bowl on clean ground and perform a prostration as previously explained.
Second, one should observe whether it is early or late in the day, and either return quickly or stop along the way;
third, one should take the teacher’s bowl and follow behind the teacher.
This is the rule for mutual dependence during the course of the meal.
When joining together for the alms-meal, there are two matters:
first, if the teacher’s bowl lacks curds, ghee, or broth, one should take the food from the bowl one has received and offer it to the teacher.
If the teacher does not take it, one should withdraw and stand back.

Second, slowly take half of the food from the teacher’s bowl and place it on clean ground upon leaves; then, taking half of the food from one’s own bowl, place it into the teacher’s bowl and withdraw to stand back.
This is the rule for when exchanging alms-food from one's bowl.
There are three matters regarding the exchange of alms-food:
first, if the teacher receives superior food in his bowl while one receives inferior food oneself, one should immediately offer it to the teacher;
Second, if the teacher wishes to trade for the bowl, one should decline and not accept it;
third, if the teacher insists on trading for the bowl, one should take a second meal, then wipe the bowl and return it to the teacher.
This is the rule for when trading alms-food.
When facing the meal, there are three matters:
first, one should present the teacher’s bowl and then sit back to eat.
Second, one should frequently observe what the teacher desires to receive, and immediately rise to fetch and give it;
third, when eating, one must neither be too hurried nor too slow; having finished, one should rise and again ask, "What else do you wish to have?"
The teacher says, "Take it away," and then one should take it away;
this is the rule for the time of receiving food.
There are three matters regarding the times before and after the meal:
First, having handed over the teacher’s bowl and requisites, one should withdraw to a secluded place and remain there; upon hearing the teacher’s call, one should immediately respond.
Second, one should beforehand take up washing water and set it to one side.
Third, when the teacher has finished eating, one should wash the teacher’s hands and then withdraw;
when the teacher instructs one to leave the meal, one should then perform a prostration before departing from the meal.
These are the rules for the sequence of actions during the time of eating.
"After the meal, there are three matters regarding the washing of the bowl:
First, having finished rinsing the mouth, one should first take the teacher’s bowl, wash it until it is clean, and place it upon a leaf of a tree.

Second, having set it aside and washed one's own bowl, one should likewise place it upon a leaf; then, taking the teacher’s bowl first, rub it with the hands until it is clean and dry, place it inside the bag, and present it to the teacher."
Third, one should take up one’s own bowl, wipe it until dry, place it inside its bag, and carry it with one while staying put.
This is the rule for when washing the bowl.
Regarding the rule for when departing after washing the bowl, there are three matters:
First, the teacher says:
"I now wish to go to such-and-such a place; you, worthy one, should return first.
Second, he prostrates himself with his head to the ground in salutation and then departs.
Third, when returning alone, one must not go through other villages to engage in play or laughter; one should return directly to one's original place to recite the scriptures.
This is the rule for departing after washing the alms bowl.
“There are five matters for a śrāmaṇera entering the assembly:
first, he should clearly study;
second, he should practice the tasks.”
Third, one must provide for the community;
fourth, one must bestow items upon the Great Śramaṇa;
fifth, when wishing to receive the full precepts, the three masters are easily found.
"Furthermore, there are five matters:
first, one should pay homage to the Buddha;
second, one should pay homage to the Sangha of bhikṣus."
Third, one should inquire after the health of those seated above and below;
fourth, one should leave a seat for the senior monk;
fifth, one must not dispute over a seat.
"Furthermore, there are five matters:
first, one must not call out to or laugh with others from across the seats;
second, one must not rise and leave frequently."
Third, if someone in the assembly calls out by name, "Śrāmaṇera so-and-so," you must immediately rise and respond;
fourth, you must follow the instructions of the Saṃgha;
fifth, when the *karmadāna* (steward) calls you to perform some task, you must return and inform your teacher.
This is called the proper procedure for entering the assembly.
There are five matters concerning a śrāmaṇera serving as the day’s duty:
first, he must cherish the property of the Saṃgha; [and so forth].
Second, one must not perform work in the middle of a path;
third, once work has begun, one must not leave midway until it is finished;
fourth, if the upādhyāya or ācārya calls for you, you must not go immediately, but should instead inform the karmadāna.
Fifth, one must follow the instructions and commands of the *mamaṭi* (steward) and must not disobey them.
This is the rule for serving as the duty-day officer (*zhīrì*).
"There are five matters regarding the selection of vegetables: [text continues]"
First, one should remove the roots;
second, one should cut them level with the head;
third, one must not allow any green or yellow parts to remain joined together.
Fourth, when washing vegetables, one should change the water three times to ensure they are clean, and then shake them three times to remove the water;
fifth, when a task is completed, one should sweep the area to leave it clean.
"Furthermore, there are five matters:
first, one must not privately take property belonging to the Sangha;
second, if one wishes to take anything, one must inform the *karmadāna*."
Third, one should exhaust one's efforts in performing the various duties for the Sangha;
fourth, one should sweep the dining hall and then arrange the mats and clear the tables;
fifth, one should sweep the area behind the quarters morning and evening, replenish the water supply, and discard ashes and soil.
"There are ten matters regarding the drawing of water:
first, if the hands are not clean, one must not immediately use them to draw water; one should first wash the hands.
Second, one must not throw the bucket into the well with great force so that it makes a sound."
Third, one should lower the bucket slowly; one must not strike it forcefully against the sides of the well so that it makes a sound.
Fourth, one must not allow the end of the rope to re-enter the well with a thud.
Fifth, one must not place one’s sandals upon the railing of the well.
Sixth, one must not take water from a jar and pour it into a cauldron;
seventh, one must not set a jar on the ground;
eighth, one should wash the bathing vessel until it is clean.
Ninth, when lifting the water vessel to enter [the dwelling], one should proceed slowly;
tenth, one must stay in a secluded place and not obstruct the path of others.
There are five matters regarding the washing cauldron:
First, one should wash the rim of the cauldron on the outside;
second, one should wash the rim of the cauldron on the inside;
third, one should wash the waist and belly [of the cauldron].
Fourth, one should wash the interior bottom;
fifth, one should change the water three times.
There are five matters regarding the blowing of the stove:
First, one must not squat while blowing on a fire;
second, one must not burn green firewood;
third, one must not burn damp firewood upside down.
Fourth, one must not burn rotten firewood;
fifth, one must not extinguish a fire by pouring hot water over it.
There are five matters regarding the sweeping of the ground:
First, one should proceed in accordance with the proper sequence;
second, when sprinkling the ground, there must be no unevenness in thickness;
third, one must not allow splashes to soil the four walls.
Fourth, one must not step on wet ground and thereby damage it;
fifth, having finished sweeping, one should immediately gather up the grass and refuse and discard them.
When a *śrāmaṇera* sweeps the floor while the community of monks is eating, there are five matters [to attend to]:
First, one must always walk backward;
second, one must not pick up soil with one's hand;
third, one must not pass beyond six people while making a mound of soil.
Fourth, it is virtuous to sweep everywhere thoroughly;
fifth, one should immediately sweep with one's own hands and carry the debris out to discard it.
There are five matters regarding the pouring of water from a water-vessel for washing:
First, one hand shall hold the top and the other hand shall hold the bottom; they must not be exchanged.
Second, one should remain close to the left side, holding [the vessel] firmly and gazing straight ahead.
Third, one should watch the person’s hand as they pour the water; it must be neither too much nor too little, but poured exactly into the person’s hand.
Fourth, when pouring water, it should be held four finger-widths below the person's hand; it must be neither too high nor too low, and one should observe the amount of water being poured.
If there is not enough water for one person, more water should be added, but the person's hand must not be obstructed.
Fifth, having washed one's hands, one should put on the *kāṣāya* robe according to the Dharma.
There are five matters regarding the carrying of the wash-basin:
first, one must not drag the basin so that it makes a sound.
Second, one should firmly hold the left side with both hands;
third, one should follow the height of the person's hand and must not look left or right;
fourth, when the basin is full of water, one should pour it out and discard it, and must not splash it on the ground in front of others.
Fifth, having finished washing one's hands, one should put on the *kāṣāya* robe again according to the Dharma.
There are five matters regarding the holding of the hand-towel:
first, one should hold the lower end with the left hand and the upper end with the right hand when handing it to another.
Second, one should remain two chi away from one's seat and must not lean against another's knee;
third, when holding a hand-towel, one must not use it to obstruct another's mouth;

fourth, when someone has finished wiping their hands, one must not take the towel away until they have released it; thereafter, one should hold it to return it to the owner or place it back in its original location.
Fifth, having washed one's hands, one should put on the *kāṣāya* robe according to the Dharma.
Regarding the cloth sandals, there are five matters:
first, one should first shake them out to remove whatever is inside;
Second, one should rise from one's seat when the senior monk approaches;
third, one should show the master the basin from behind so that he may recognize it himself;
fourth, one must not take the left hand and place it on the right; in all such matters, the śrāmaṇera should maintain a humble and respectful attitude.
Fifth, when the meal is finished, one should return, wash one's hands, and put on the *kāṣāya* robe according to the Dharma.
There are seven matters regarding a *śrāmaṇera* washing his bowl:
first, if there is leftover rice in the bowl, one must not simply take it up and discard it.
Second, when one wishes to discard the rice from the middle of the bowl, it should be placed on clean ground;
third, one should use cleansing beans or grass leaves;
fourth, when washing the bowl, one must not do so on clean ground or in a place frequented by people.
Fifth, when washing the bowl, one should ensure that the base remains visible;
sixth, one should add fresh, clean water, and must not discard the wastewater far away so as to splash people;
seventh, when wishing to discard the water from the bowl, one should hold it four inches above the ground, ensuring there is no unevenness in height.
"There are five matters regarding the wiping of the alms bowl:
first, one should wash one's hands again and wipe them until they are dry;
second, one should hold a clean hand-towel and place it upon one's knees."
Third, one should wipe the interior until it is dry;
fourth, once the exterior has been wiped by hand, one may no longer wipe the interior;
fifth, when the bowl is dry, one should immediately take a clean cloth to cover it, place it in its bag, and set it in its usual location.
"When attending a communal meal, there are five matters for instructing a śrāmaṇera on how to hold his alms-bowl:
first, he must not place it on the ground;
second, he must not stack them so that they make a sound."
Third, one must not place willow twigs inside the alms bowl;
fourth, when someone comes to present a table, one must not prop the bowl against that person’s table;

fifth, one must not hand the bowl from behind a person, but should instead proceed directly in front of them; furthermore, one should not walk through the midst of the assembly; once the teacher has finished eating, one should rise, take the bowl, and return to one’s seat.
This is the method for carrying the alms bowl.
"When sent by one's teacher to deliver a message of thanks, there are seven matters to observe:
first, one should go directly."
Second, one should return directly;
third, one should remember what the teacher says and also remember the responses given by others;
fourth, one must not pass through places indiscriminately.
Fifth, if one cannot obtain what was sought, one must not remain to stay overnight;
sixth, one must not engage in frivolous chatter;
seventh, when going out, one must act according to the proper rules.
“A śrāmaṇera who has not yet finished his service for the community of bhikṣus must not enter the gate of the Great Śramaṇa’s dwelling arbitrarily.
There are three circumstances under which he may enter:
first, if he is temporarily sent by his upādhyāya or ācārya;”
Second, if one has been hired for labor;
third, if one wishes to go and inquire about the scriptures and ought to enter.
There are seven matters regarding the desire to enter a doorway:
First, one must snap the fingers three times before being permitted to enter;
second, one must not stand or sit directly in the path of people, nor obstruct the light of the lamps;
third, one must not speak falsely regarding other matters.
Fourth, one should join the palms and speak according to the Dharma;
fifth, if instructed to sit, one must not cross one's legs;
sixth, one must not be frivolous or sarcastic.

Seventh, one must not obstruct others who are ahead; when wishing to leave a door, one should face the door to exit, turning toward it and stepping back as one goes out, rather than walking away with one's back turned.
"When you send a śrāmaṇera on a distant journey, you should instruct him on three preliminary matters:
first, if someone asks you, 'What is the name of your upādhyāya? you should reply, 'His name is So-and-so.'"
Second, he asked again, "How many years has your preceptor been a śramaṇa? and [the disciple] replied, "For so many years.
Third, he asked again, "What kind of person is your preceptor? and [the disciple] replied, "A man from such-and-such a commandery and county."
If they were further to ask you, "What is the name of your preceptor? you should reply, "His name is So-and-so.
If they were further to ask, "How old is your preceptor? you should reply, "He is such-and-such years of age."
If he further asks, "What kind of person is your preceptor? one should reply, "He is a man from such-and-such a country and district.
If he further asks, "What is the name of the worthy one? one should reply, "His name is so-and-so."
He asked again, "How long has it been since you became a śrāmaṇera? and he replied, "For several years, several months, several days, and several hours.
This constitutes knowing one's upādhyāya and ācārya, as well as knowing one's own time, name, age, month, and day.
"There are five matters regarding entering the bathhouse:
first, enter with the head bowed;
second, upon entering, one should avoid the place of the senior monk."
Third, when the elder is reciting the scriptures, one must not engage in idle chatter;
fourth, one must not splash water at one another;
fifth, one must not extinguish a fire by pouring water upon it.
"Furthermore, there are five matters:
first, one must not engage in idle chatter or mockery;
second, one must not break the large jars or small pots within."
Third, one must not waste water;
fourth, one must not wash face-powder or use sesame oil in the water;
fifth, one should depart quickly and must not remain there to wash clothes.
"When a śrāmaṇera walks behind the house, there are ten matters:
first, when one wishes to defecate or urinate, one should go immediately;
second, while walking, one must not look left or right."
Third, upon arriving at the gate, one should snap the fingers three times;
fourth, one must not urge the person inside to come out;
fifth, having already arrived above, one should again snap the fingers three times.
Sixth, one must not swallow loudly;
seventh, one must not lower the head to look at the private parts;
eighth, one must not play with the dust and ash above.
Ninth, one must not take water and pour it upon the walls;
tenth, having returned, one should wash one's hands, for until one has washed them, one should not hold any object.
Furthermore, there are five other matters:
First, one must not spit directly upon the wall in front;
second, one must not look around to the left or right;
third, one must not take grass and draw upon the walls or the floor.
Fourth, one must not hold a torch to draw lines on the ground or on walls;
fifth, one must not remain for a long time in a latrine.
One should descend from it oneself; if one should encounter someone there, one must not perform a prostration, but should instead yield the path and depart.
Having finished explaining the seventy-two rules of decorum for śrāmaṇeras, there are fourteen matters in total.
The teacher speaks to them as follows:
There are two matters:
first, one must not reply;
second, one must not explain oneself.
There are ten matters regarding a *śrāmaṇera* prostrating to his preceptor:
first, one should not prostrate when there is a bowl before the preceptor’s head;
second, one should not prostrate when the preceptor is sitting in meditation.
Third, one should not perform prostrations while the teacher is walking in meditation;
fourth, one should not perform prostrations while the teacher is eating;
fifth, one should not perform prostrations while the teacher is preaching the sutras.
Sixth, when meeting one's teacher, one should not perform a prostration while on the left side;
seventh, one should not perform a prostration while the teacher is brushing their teeth;
eighth, when wishing to enter the room to perform a prostration, one should snap the fingers three times; if the teacher does not respond, one should depart.
Ninth, one must not be more than seven paces away from the teacher;
tenth, when the teacher’s door opens, one should perform a prostration.
When entering the room early in the morning, there are five matters to attend to:
First, arrange the robes;
second, remove the bowls;
third, sweep the floor.
Fourth is inquiring about the sūtras;
fifth is giving material things.
There are five matters regarding the folding of the three robes:
First, one must not stand directly in front;
second, one should stand on the left side;
third, one must recognize the inner and outer sides of the robe.
Fourth, one must not fold it upside down;
fifth, one should place it in its regular location.
There are five matters regarding following the teacher:
First, one must not pass by people's houses;
second, one must not stop on the road to converse with others;
third, one must not look left and right.
Fourth, one should keep the head lowered while following behind the teacher;
fifth, upon arriving at the house of a donor (*dānapati*), one should stand to one side until the teacher instructs one to sit.
There are five matters regarding providing what the teacher requires:
First, one should obtain willow twigs;
second, one should obtain cleansing powder;
third, one must not keep water overnight.
Fourth, one should draw water again;
fifth, hand towels should be washed clean when used.
There are five matters regarding a śrāmaṇera’s washing:
First, one must not face a stūpa;
second, one must not face one's upādhyāya;
third, one must not face one's ācārya.
Fourth, one should do so in a secluded place;
fifth, one should fetch water for oneself and must not take water that has been prepared by another.
There are five matters regarding entering the door at dusk:
First, one should sweep and clean the bedding;
second, one should arrange the robes and coverlets;
third, one should put away the bowls.
Fourth, one should naturally light the lamps;
fifth, when teaching others how to lie down, one should depart;
and when leaving, one should turn one's back toward them, pull the door, and close it.
There are five matters for a śrāmaṇera when receiving the sūtras from his teacher:
first, to adjust his robes;
second, to join his palms in salutation.
Third, one must not lean forward or backward;
fourth, the two feet should be level;
fifth, one should maintain a slight stoop.
There are five matters regarding a śrāmaṇera presenting the three robes to his preceptor:
first, he should wash his hands;
second, he should present the antarvāsaka.
Third, one should provide an *antarvāsaka*;
fourth, one should provide a *saṃghāṭī*;
fifth, one should provide a hand-towel.
There are five matters concerning a śrāmaṇera washing his bowl:
first, one must obtain cow-dung ash;
second, one must obtain cleansing powder.
Third, it should be held seven inches above the ground;
fourth, there must be no sound, one should change the water three times, and when discarding the water, one must not sprinkle it on the ground;
fifth, it should be kept dry.
There are five matters regarding a śrāmaṇera sweeping the ground:
first, one must not sweep with one's back turned toward the teacher;
second, one must not sweep against the grain.
Third, one should ensure it is clean;
fourth, there must be no footprints left behind;
fifth, one should discard it immediately.
When a śrāmaṇera accompanies his preceptor to the house of a donor (dānapati), there are five matters to attend to:
first, he should carry the alms bowl;
second, he should carry a hand-towel.
Third, one should knock at the door;
fourth, upon arriving at the house of a donor, one should request pure water to wash the bowl;
fifth, when the teacher is seated, one should take the hand-towel and the bowl and present them to the teacher, and only then should one return to sit down oneself.
When a śrāmaṇera enters the bathhouse, there are five matters to observe:
first, he must not enter before his teacher;
second, he must not sit in front of his teacher.
Third, one must not move until the teacher has obtained water;
fourth, if one wishes to rub the teacher’s back, one should first signal the intention;
fifth, after bathing, one should first take up the robe to be worn.
Regarding the etiquette and dignified demeanor of a śrāmaṇera, as well as the morning and evening inquiries and prostrations, there are thirteen matters:
first, one should rise early to wash and rinse;
second, one should properly adjust one’s robes.
Third, one should inquire after his health and well-being;
fourth, if the teacher is inside and one wishes to enter, one must first remove whatever is worn upon the head and whatever is worn on the feet;
fifth, one must not tread upon another's footprints.
Sixth, one should stand outside for three finger-snap intervals, then call out before entering;
seventh, one should prostrate with the head and face touching the ground as a salutation;
eighth, if commanded to sit, one should yield three times before sitting down.
Ninth, one must always sit with dignified composure;
tenth, when questioned, one should respond immediately with clear and distinct speech;
eleventh, when there is nothing to say, one should remain silent.
Twelfth, when the business is finished and one must withdraw, one should prostrate as at the beginning;
thirteenth, when wishing to leave the room, one should turn the body back toward the teacher before departing.
Furthermore, there are fifteen matters regarding the *śrāmaṇera* holding the teacher’s water vessel:
First, one should clean the bathing flask;
second, it should have a fixed place;
third, one should ensure it is filled with pure water.
Fourth, one must not keep water overnight;
fifth, one should prepare *śākhā* (tooth-sticks) in advance;
sixth, one should treat the *śākhā* in accordance with the Dharma.
Seventh, the water pitcher should be held one chi above the knee;
eighth, when holding the pitcher, the left hand should grasp the top while the right hand supports the bottom;
ninth, when pouring water, one must ensure the amount is properly adjusted to be neither too much nor too little.
Tenth, one must not allow any sound to be made;
eleventh, the hand-towel must always have its fixed place;
twelfth, when holding the towel, hold it in the left hand and present it to the teacher with the right hand.
Thirteenth, one should have a fixed place for discarding impure water;
fourteenth, one must not allow it to splash onto clean ground;
fifteenth, after using a cloth, one should return it to its usual place.
Furthermore, there are eight matters regarding the sweeping and wiping of the bed:
first, one must always face toward the honored one;
second, one must not turn one's back to them.
Third, when sprinkling water on the ground, one should use a light hand and measure the amount of water;
fourth, when using a dustpan, one should face toward oneself;
fifth, when discarding waste, there should be a fixed place for it.
Sixth, sweep and wipe the beds and mats;
seventh, fold the robes, bedding, and pillows;
eighth, sweep and wipe the beds so as not to make any noise.
Furthermore, there are fourteen matters regarding the carrying of the teacher’s food:
first, one must prepare a clean cloth;
second, when intending to present the food, one must always support it with both hands as it is lowered.
Third, one should proceed straight ahead;
fourth, one should kneel to present [the items] to the teacher;
fifth, one must not engage in conversation or laughter with others along the way.
Sixth, one must not make noise while serving food;
seventh, all food and drink served should be appropriate in temperature, neither too cold nor too hot;
eighth, the spoons and chopsticks should be kept clean and pure.
Ninth, whatever benefit there may be, one must ensure it is distributed with perfect balance;
tenth, when dwelling, one must have a fixed place;
eleventh, one should be dignified and upright.
Twelfth, when the meal is finished, one should carefully and slowly clear away the utensils;
thirteenth, one should lift them up in their proper order;
fourteenth, one should sweep and wash the utensils exactly according to the usual rules.
Furthermore, there are ten matters regarding the taking up of the Dharma robes and sandals:
first, one should hold the upper part with the left hand and the lower part with the right;
second, one should kneel before presenting them to the teacher.
Third, one should fold the *kāṣāya*; it must not be held in the mouth.
Fourth, one must not shake it so that it makes a sound.
Fifth, one should return it to its usual place.
Sixth, cover [the shoes] with a cloth;
seventh, when taking up one's sandals, one should first shake them out;
eighth, one must not allow loud noises to occur.
Ninth, when placing it on the ground, one should ensure it is upright;
tenth, one should return it to its original place.
There are eight matters regarding the taking up of the alms bowl (*pātra*) and the water flask (*kuṇḍikā*):
First, rub and wipe it clean beforehand;
second, support its base with both hands;
third, kneel to receive the teacher's bowl.
Fourth, when washing, one should use soapberry pods and bean powder;
fifth, once finished, one should dry them in one's hands;
sixth, if there is urgent business requiring travel, it is appropriate to wear them in the sunlight.
Seventh, if one approaches a fire, one should cause it to dry;
eighth, having finished, one should restore it to its usual place.
Regarding the taking up of the mendicant’s staff (*khakkhara*), there are seven matters:
First, one should sweep and wipe it until it is clean;
second, one must not let it touch the ground below;
third, one must not point or gesture with it toward anything.
Fourth, do not allow any sound to be made;
fifth, one should hold it with both hands;
sixth, one should kneel to present it to the teacher.
Seventh, he shall finally return to his usual place.
Furthermore, when attending to the teacher’s bathing and shaving of the head, he should wear the dharma robes in the morning; there are twelve matters regarding this:
first, he must diligently maintain reverence and perform what is appropriate.
Second, adjusting the temperature according to the season;
third, sweeping and cleaning the bathhouse;
fourth, providing pure hot water.
Fifth, one should first prepare soap pods, cleansing powder, and sesame oil;
sixth, one should pre-arrange a clean hand-towel;
seventh, one should provide a brazier for fire in case of cold.
Eighth, one should remain standing upright outside and not allow others to enter;
ninth, if shaving the hair, one must ensure it is done in a regular place;
tenth, if airing out the Dharma robes, one should wait until they are dry.
Eleventh, when departing on urgent business, one must entrust matters to someone else so that they are not forgotten upon one's departure;
twelfth, when concluding one’s duties, one must ensure that everything is returned to its proper place.
Furthermore, there are seven matters regarding the offering of incense and flowers:
first, one should thoroughly wipe the incense burner;
second, one should discard the flowers from the previous night.
Third, one should adjust the amount of incense burned;
fourth, when distributing incense and flowers, one should begin with the senior monk (upādhyāya);
fifth, when distributing the incense, the hands of those receiving it should remain five inches apart.
Sixth, one should not hold an incense burner without using it to perfume oneself;
seventh, it should ultimately be placed in its permanent location.
Furthermore, there are eight matters regarding the lighting of a lamp:
First, remove the old wick;
second, scrub and wash the lamp-stand until it is clean;
third, properly adjust the oil container.
Fourth, seek out pure wicks;
fifth, do not allow the oil to run out, but go to replenish it as needed;
sixth, one should rise early in the morning to inspect and protect [the lamp].
Seventh, when the oil is not yet exhausted, one should support the remaining wick and move it to a place where it can lean, lighting it separately until it is finished;
eighth, finally, one should slowly return it to its original place.
If one goes to gather flowers or take willow branches, there are nine matters to attend to:
first, if there is an owner, inquire of that owner;
second, if there is no owner, one should offer prayers for the deities of the mountains, marshes, and trees.
Third, when taking flowers or willow twigs, one must not pull up their roots or stumps;
fourth, on the road, one should proceed directly back and forth;
fifth, one must not speak with negligence or engage in idle play.
Sixth, even if you are wronged by others, be careful never to associate with them;
seventh, lower your head and reproach yourself within, ensuring that no resentment arises;
eighth, if you wish to offer flowers, you should begin with the senior monk at the head of the assembly.
Ninth, one must remove withered flowers.
In all that one undertakes, one must not act according to one's own will; there are eighteen matters [to be observed]:
first, when entering or leaving, coming or going, one must first inform the teacher.
Second, if one wishes to stay overnight elsewhere, one should first inform the teacher;
third, if one is making a new Dharma robe, one should first inform the teacher;
fourth, if one wishes to wear a new Dharma robe, one should first inform the teacher and receive permission from him.
Fifth, if one wishes to wash the Dharma robes, one should first inform the teacher;
sixth, if one wishes to shave one's head, one should first inform the teacher;
seventh, if one is ill and takes medicine, one should first inform the teacher.
Eighth, if one is to perform affairs for the Sangha, one must first inform the teacher before departing;
ninth, if one wishes to privately possess items such as paper and pens, one must first inform the teacher;
tenth, if one is to chant sutras or hymns, one must first inform the teacher.
Eleventh: If one receives a gift of goods from another, one must first inform the teacher before accepting it;
twelfth: when giving one's own goods to others, one should first inform the teacher, and only give them after the teacher has granted permission;
thirteenth: when someone requests a loan from oneself, one must inform the teacher for each instance, and only lend it after the teacher has granted permission.
Fourteenth: When one wishes to borrow anything from another person, one must inform the teacher; only if the teacher grants permission may one go. Fifteenth:
Regarding the protocol for making a request, one should first adjust one’s robes and perform a prostration as a sign of respect.
Sixteenth: Whether the request is granted or denied, one must in all cases remain reverent and perform a prostration.
Seventeenth, one should state what one wishes to know;
eighteenth, one must not harbor resentment when responding with words in reply.
Furthermore, there are sixteen matters regarding returning from following a teacher on a journey, whether going first or returning last:
First, one should adjust one's robes;
second, one should understand the intent of what is said and always respond with proper courtesy, following those who carry the mendicant’s staff and hand-towel;
third, one should follow behind the teacher.
Fourth, one must not step on another's shadow;
fifth, one must not brandish a *khakkhara* staff in front of them;
sixth, one must not converse with others while walking on the road.
Seventh, one must not harbor ill will toward a teacher who has committed a transgression;
eighth, if the teacher sends one back to retrieve something, one should follow the path by which he came;
ninth, one should immediately act according to his instructions.
Tenth, be careful not to linger;
eleventh, if the teacher sends you to stay and preach the sutras for a donor, you must immediately prostrate yourself and receive his instructions;
twelfth, you should return early in the evening.
Thirteenth, one must be careful never to stay overnight;
fourteenth, upon returning, one should invite [the teacher] to receive his greetings and inquire after his affairs, first arranging one's robes;
fifteenth, one should prostrate oneself with the five limbs touching the ground to pay homage.
Sixteenth, one should pay respects to the teacher according to the usual rules.
When traveling alone to attend a funeral, visit the sick, or similar occasions, there are nine matters to observe:

First, upon reaching the host’s gate, one should observe the proper etiquette of advancing and retreating; if there is a separate seat, one should sit there, but if no separate seat is provided, it is inappropriate to sit among the others.
Second, one should observe one's seat and sit upright, avoiding what is improper or forbidden;
third, if someone wishes to inquire about the sutras, one should know the proper time;
fourth, one must be careful never to engage in discourse at an inappropriate time.
Fifth, when the host provides food, even if it is not food for a formal assembly at the prescribed time, one must not allow the ritual procedures to be neglected;
sixth, one should return by the end of the day;
seventh, one must not commit the offense of traveling at night.
Eighth, if it is near dusk or there is a violent wind and rain, one should act according to the exigencies of the moment;
ninth, upon returning, everything should be restored as it was before.
If one encounters the teacher on the road, there are six matters to attend to:
First, one should first adjust one's robes;
second, one should remove one's leather sandals;
third, when paying homage to the teacher, one should prostrate oneself at his feet.
Fourth, one should follow behind the teacher;
fifth, if the teacher departs elsewhere, one should prostrate and receive his instructions;
sixth, even when not accompanying the teacher, one must ensure that all ritual observances remain as they were.
When the Sangha is eating rice, there are sixteen matters:
first, upon hearing the sound of the *gandi*, one should immediately adjust one’s robes;
second, one should strive to remove leather footwear and proceed to stay beneath the stupa.
Third, one must always maintain a dignified and upright demeanor;
fourth, if one arrives after the teacher and takes one's seat, one must be careful not to speak or laugh as others are engaged in conversation;
fifth, when a superior person recites the sutras or offers prayers of blessing, one should show reverence and be cautious not to lose proper decorum.
Sixth, at the beginning of a meal, one should first look around above and below;
seventh, one should not eat before the assembly, nor stop eating after the assembly;
eighth, one should not criticize the food as being good or bad.
Ninth, one must not eat large mouthfuls or small mouthfuls;
tenth, one must be careful never to swallow too large a gulp;
eleventh, one must not excessively stir or scrape within the alms bowl.
Twelfth, one must not strike the table with the chopsticks;
thirteenth, one must not seek to receive more than one's share;
fourteenth, one must not privately give food to others or pick out portions to give to a dog.
Fifteenth: If someone comes to offer more food, one must not say, "I do not need it.
Sixteenth: If one says one is already full, one should use the hand to signal them to withdraw.

Furthermore, when the assembly of monks recites the sutras, there are thirteen matters to consider: whether it is at a Dharma assembly where the sutra is being preached, in a warm room (*jantāghara*) or a cool room (*prāsādaka-śālā*), or in a bathhouse (*snāna-śālā*).
First, one should adjust one's robes;
second, one should walk straight ahead with a level gaze;
third, one must not converse or laugh with others while on the road.
Fourth, pay respects to those who are honored in due order;
fifth, withdraw and sit on the seats in pairs;
sixth, when the elder recites the sutra, take one's seat according to rank.
Seventh, one must always sit with dignified composure;
eighth, one must be careful not to engage in idle chatter;
ninth, one must not cough or spit loudly.
Tenth, one must not spit on clean ground, as this violates the rules of decorum;
eleventh, if it is one’s turn to preach the sutras, one should do so immediately;
twelfth, when appointed by the assembly to ascend the high seat, one must first examine one’s deportment and conduct with care, being cautious not to lose dignity.
Thirteenth: If there is a lapse in propriety during the assembly, one should suppress evil and promote the good; take care never to manifest such negligence.
Furthermore, regarding the thirteen matters concerning the Sangha’s recitation of the sutras, as well as the turn of duty, the day-watch, and the performance of rites at dawn and dusk:
first, upon hearing the sound of the *ghanṭā*, one should prepare the incense and lamps in advance.
Second, one should apply incense as before;
third, one should arrange things in their proper order;
fourth, one should sweep and dust the beds and mats.
Fifth, sweep and sprinkle the area according to the Dharma;
sixth, when the Dharma assembly concludes, clearly hand over all items under one's charge to the donors for their appropriate use;
seventh, once the task is finished and the items have been received back, restore everything to its original state.
Eighth, the keys shall be handed over; the door shall be closed early and opened late as a constant rule.
Ninth, if there are unexpected guests, they shall listen to the instructions from the Master’s side, and whatever they require shall be provided.
Tenth, if there are guests staying overnight, they shall all adjust their robes and take their positions in the usual places.
Eleventh, when confronted, one should respond clearly and with distinct articulation;
twelfth, one must remain upright and dignified at all times, never allowing one’s decorum to falter;
thirteenth, if one wishes to go out briefly, one should immediately have another person take one’s place, so as not to leave the position vacant and cause others to call out repeatedly.

Furthermore, those on duty must oversee the ten subsequent matters; if one serves as a duty-holder, they should properly follow the established protocols for their practice, which include various tasks and labors:
first, the construction of stupas;
second, the arrangement of all matters concerning the lecture hall and the Sangha.
Third, if one is making a Buddha image, one should always rise early and attend to the necessary tasks with care;
fourth, one should select appropriate tools—such as files, axes, and saws—and ensure they are kept in their proper places;
fifth, if red pigments, lacquer, glue, or ink are to be used for painting, one should prepare them in advance so that there is no lack when the time comes.
Sixth, when the selection and recording of texts are completed, they must have a permanent location;
seventh, as the original scriptures are few, one must clearly record the number of those received and transmit them with precision, ensuring there is no error or omission;
ninth, regarding all acquisitions for one's residence, one must consult the *māmaka* (steward).
Tenth, regarding the application of these [precepts] so that others may proclaim and enumerate them, ensuring they possess both beginning and end:
furthermore, there are sixteen matters concerning solitary alms-gathering (*piṇḍapāta*).
When practicing alms-gathering, the first is to strive to be accompanied by others.
Second, if there is no one else present, one should know the place where the alms-bowl may be set down;
third, the bowl should always rest against the left side of the body;
fourth, regarding the proper manner of carrying the bowl, when going out, it should be held with the opening facing outward.
Fifth, when returning with food, one should keep it directed inward;
sixth, upon arriving at a person's gate, one should carefully examine one's conduct;
seventh, if there are no men in the house, one should be cautious not to enter.
Eighth, if one wishes to sit, one should first inspect the seat;
ninth, if there are weapons on the seat, one should not sit upon it;
tenth, if there are precious objects on the seat, one should not sit upon it.
Eleventh: If there are women present with their robes and ornaments, one should not sit; even if none are present, one should nevertheless sit.
Twelfth: The host provides food. Thirteenth:
Upon eating, one should offer a prayer of aspiration.
Fourteenth, one must not inquire about the quality or excellence of the food;
fifteenth, one must not preach the sutras before eating;
sixteenth, even if one wishes to preach the sutras, one should know the appropriate time for preaching and the inappropriate time for preaching.
Furthermore, there are nine matters to be observed when seeking things in the marketplace:
first, one should keep the head bowed and proceed straight forward or return directly;
second, if one beholds strange objects, one must be careful not to examine them closely.
Third, one should not engage in disputes regarding social status, whether high or low;
fourth, one should not sit in a woman's shop;
fifth, if one is wronged by another, one should skillfully avoid it and not seek retribution from them.
Sixth, in buying and selling, if one has paid the price according to the truth and there is no word for taking it back, yet one repeatedly returns to demand it;
seventh, having already promised an item to someone, even if another appears at a lower price, one must not abandon the former to take the latter, thereby causing the original owner resentment;

eighth, if one sees members of the fourfold assembly engaged in buying or selling at an undervalued price, one should not leave them to their own devices, but should speak according to the Dharma, saying that such a thing is not permissible.
Ninth, one must be careful not to act as a guarantor, thereby incurring blame or liability.
Furthermore, there are nine matters regarding entering a bhikṣuṇī monastery. If the teacher sends one to a bhikṣuṇī monastery: first, one should go together with them;
second, one should circumambulate the stūpa and pay homage exactly according to the usual rules.
Third, if there is another seat available, one must not sit where no other seat exists;
fourth, when one is ill and wishes to inquire about the sutras, one should speak only what is appropriate to say;
fifth, one must not engage in discourse at an improper time.
Sixth, one must not return another's faults;
seventh, if one is offered precious or unusual garments, headcloths, or footwear as a gift, one must not accept even a single item;
eighth, if one returns such things, one must not speak of their quality, whether good or bad.
Ninth, others must not say, "This is used solely for making offerings to such-and-such [deity].
Furthermore, there are eight matters regarding the lecturing on sutras and the recitation of the Dharma:

First, one must ensure that the presentation is thorough and precise; this is because what people perceive may differ, as various individuals on the left and right may each have their own habitual training.
Second, be careful never to claim exclusive knowledge by asserting that this is right and that is wrong;
third, when disputes arise among fellow students, strive to bring about reconciliation and ensure no partiality remains;
fourth, regarding communal duties and labor, be careful never to substitute for others in order to display your own merit.
Fifth, when the Great Śramaṇa recites the precepts, you must be careful not to gaze at him;
sixth, if you know you have committed an offense against the assembly, you should immediately speak of it to repent and reach reconciliation with them;
seventh, if the teacher asks you:
"If someone says you have committed a transgression,
you should immediately report the matter as it is;
eighth, do not conceal anything so as to incur guilt."
There is a discourse on ten matters: one should constantly recite the sutras and practice the Way during the three periods of day and night. First, one should adjust one's robes;
second, if one practices walking meditation (caṅkrama), it must be done in a fixed location;
third, one should do so in the center [of that place].
Fourth, within the lecture hall;
fifth, beneath a stūpa;
sixth, likewise within the refectory.
Seventh, one must not step in leather sandals;
eighth, one must not wear wooden clogs;
ninth, one must not carry a staff.
Tenth, one must be careful never to recite the sutras while lying down.

Furthermore, there are ten matters regarding the practice of reciting the sutras while walking, which are the constant rules for the dwelling quarters: first, sleeping and resting shall be separate and not intermingled;
second, one must receive the correct phrasing and reading of the sutra texts.
Third, to discuss the meaning of the sutras;
fourth, to inquire after one's illness;
fifth, to go there for some other purpose.
Sixth, one must not speak of matters that are not urgent;
seventh, one must not point out the faults of others;
eighth, one must not engage in mutual criticism.
Ninth, one must be clear and explicit when borrowing or giving things;
tenth, one must not violate agreements or contracts so as to lose the trust of the Way.
This concludes the *Sāmaṇera-daśa-śīla-dharma with Dignified Deportment*, in one fascicle. Regarding the five virtues:
First, they resolve their minds to leave secular life, for they cherish and wear the Way within them;
second, they alter their physical appearance to accord with the dharma robes;
third, they forever sever affection for kin, being free from partiality toward either side.
Fourth, they cast aside their bodies and lives in order to honor and revere the Way;
fifth, they resolve to seek the Mahāyāna for the sake of delivering all beings.
As for the ten numbers:
First, all sentient beings subsist by depending on food and drink;
second, name-and-form;
third, the three types of sensation.
Fourth, the Four Noble Truths;
fifth, the Five Aggregates;
sixth, the Six Sense Bases.
Seventh, the seven factors of enlightenment;
eighth, the eightfold noble path;
ninth, the nine abodes of sentient beings.
Tenth are the ten spheres of totality (*daśa kṛtsnāyatanāni*).
